name: Carla Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing gets traced back to you. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at four, because the bus to the pit leaves the town square at half five. I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper mine, one of the big ones, 220 tonnes when it's loaded. Twelve hours going round and round: under the shovel, up the ramp, tip at the crusher, back down. I like the quiet in the cab, honestly, but my eyes are gone by the end, and the dust gets in your teeth.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years and a bit. Before that I did twenty-six years in the laundry at the district hospital, until they shipped the washing out to a contractor in the city and shut us down. The union got us a small payout and the mine was hiring, so here I am at fifty-eight, still the slowest on the ramp. My partner Tomas is a caretaker at the primary school, so between us we get by, just. There's not much saved, maybe three weeks if the truck broke down and so did we.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. I'd love to believe it. But the trucks in the north pit don't need clever AI, they just need to be cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say good, now let's talk about the north pit. Marco, our delegate, would nod and say the same as last month. To my sister I'd say don't get excited, nothing's changed for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the AI hype hardly matters to me. The self-driving trucks in the north pit don't need some genius computer, and they don't get tired at hour eleven. I'm two years in and the slowest on the ramp, so if they spread the trial, I'm on the first list, plateau or no plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down, and I'd go to every union meeting about the north pit trial. I'd try to put twenty a week aside, if the gas bill lets me. And I'd stop lending my son money for his rent, which I hate saying out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, the kind you carry in your shoulders. It's not fear of something new, it's knowing exactly what a closure letter looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would say we've been poor before and we'll be poor again, which is his idea of comfort. The school's got him for a few years yet. I'd tell Tomas I'm fine, and then I'd check the bank app in the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How close does the north pit feel, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close enough to see from the crib hut. Six driverless trucks went in last spring, and nobody's told us how long the trial runs. When the laundry closed, the first sign was the managers stopped answering questions, and they've stopped answering questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. At Red Hill that's dispatch, the people in the tower telling every truck which shovel to go to. Once a computer runs dispatch, the driverless trucks are easy to roll out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union I'd say the computers will run dispatch and planning within a couple of years, and that's the bit the driverless trucks were waiting for. I'd tell Marco we need a deal for the older drivers now, not when the letters come. Online I wouldn't say anything, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, haul trucks are the one robot that's already here, so slow robots everywhere else don't help me at all. With AI running dispatch, the north pit trial goes mine-wide in two or three years, and I'm sixty then, six years off my pension. I don't think I'd last that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marco straight away what redundancy pay looks like for someone with two years' service, because I think it's next to nothing. I'd sell the car, get the mine bus and stop helping my son with his rent. And I'd push the union for a fund, paid by the companies that automate, to bridge older workers to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at two in the morning doing sums that don't add up, same as the year the laundry shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go for a control room job if one came up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd pick the young ones, and the control room is the computer's job in this picture anyway. I can barely work the touchscreen in the cab. My friend Inés says I should try, and maybe I'd put my name down so nobody can say I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, then the TV. Then we start missing the electric by a week here and there, like we did in 2019. Tomas would pick up Saturday cleaning at the school if they'd give it to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots in 2031? The north pit trucks are already driving themselves. They don't need to wait for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say the bosses will have the computers plan the whole switch to driverless trucks by 2028, and we need a deal before they finish planning. I'd say it to Marco, our delegate, and I'd say it loudly. To my sister I'd say it's the laundry all over again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the thinking machines in 2028 do the part the managers do, the planning and the dispatch, and that makes the north pit trucks cheaper to run across the whole mine. Robots that can do anything come in 2031, but haul trucks don't need anything, they're already half there. I'd be 60 when the clever computers come and 63 when the robots do, and my pension's not till 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift going from now on and put it all toward the bills, because there's no saving on our pay, only less owing. I'd stop the car and the phone contracts and go back to a pay-as-you-go phone. I'd push Marco and the union to fight for a bridge to the pension for over-sixties before the first redundancy letters. And I'd find out exactly what government help there is for someone my age, before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going soft. I'd be counting shifts the way you count steps in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the laundry all over again. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the hospital laundry they had a consultant in for a month with a laptop, and then we got the letter. Here it'd be a computer doing the consultant's job in an afternoon. Twenty-six years of folding sheets and two years of driving, and none of it counts for anything a robot can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas's job at the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mopping floors and fixing radiators, that's hands-on, so maybe 2031 for him too. The school won't rush, they never have money for anything. If my partner Tomas keeps his caretaker job till 2031, that's the only thing between us and asking our kids for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be 66. That's my pension year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union that this is the one where we can still win something, if we start now. Five years is enough to get early pensions for the over-sixties into the agreement. I'd sign every petition and go to every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I might just make it. If the clever computers come in 2031 and the robots in 2034, I'd be 63 and then 66, and I might reach my pension before they push me out. But the north pit trucks don't care about the card, they could spread before then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save around fifty each payday and stop the lottery tickets, which Tomas says are my retirement plan. I'd push the union to bargain for early pensions for over-sixties. And I'd write to our MP for the first time in my life, asking for a pension bridge paid by the companies that bring in robot trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of hope in it. Like the last hour of a twelve-hour shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the control room course in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Inés did it with me. I'd still be slow, but five years is long enough to be slow and still get there. I don't want to be the woman who said no to the control room course and then got the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your last day if you made it to 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drive the truck up the ramp one more time and wave at the empty north pit trucks. Then I'd go home and sleep past four o'clock for the first time in nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be retired by then, if the north pit lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union that this one's about the younger drivers, not people like me. They need a plan for 2039, and they've got time to make one. I'd tell them to get it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the card doesn't scare me, the north pit does, same as in the first picture. If they spread the self-driving trucks in the next few years, the card doesn't matter. If they don't, I'd reach 66 and leave on my own two feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down. I'd pay the car off in the next two years and then put a little by each month. And I'd keep going to the union meetings, mostly for Inés and the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The big wave is far off, but the little one in the north pit is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you made it to your pension, what would worry you about the people you left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inés's girl would be out of college by then, looking for work in a town where the mine runs itself. I'd worry about the young ones having nothing to start on. Ten years is the first picture where I can see my last shift happening on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomas be all right in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's older than me, he'd be retired long before 2039. The school would give him a cake and a card. That's how it should go for everybody.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that bring in the robot trucks, and a union strong enough to make them pay it. Not a course, a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. There are eleven of us on trucks at Red Hill, and most of us came late, after the kids or after some other job closed. The mine hired us women because the trucks are easy to drive now, and the mine will fire us because the trucks are easy to drive now.

headlineQuote: The mine hired us women because the trucks are easy to drive now, and the mine will fire us because the trucks are easy to drive now.
portrait: Carla Alvarez, 58, drives **a haul truck** at the Red Hill copper mine, after twenty-six years in a hospital laundry.
She has about **three weeks of savings**, a partner who is a school caretaker, and no other mine nearby.
The **driverless trucks** on trial at her mine make her anxious even in a plateau.
Steady change and fast AGI both **alarm** her, because AI dispatch speeds those trucks up before her pension.
She turns to **the union** and a pension bridge, and only slower AGI lets her picture leaving on her terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the driverless trucks would spread years before her pension at 66.
She'd have almost **no savings** and no other mine nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A **pension bridge** for over-fifty-fives, paid by the companies that bring in robot trucks.
A **union strong enough** to win it.
